name: Bonnor's Stars of Charged Dust
description: Stars of dust in which every grain carries just enough charge for its electric repulsion to cancel its gravity, so the dust rests in equilibrium with no pressure, in a ball or in any other shape. William Bonnor built a sphere of it in 1965, and in 1975 he and S. B. P. Wickramasuriya made one whose surface lies as close to its own horizon as one likes, so that light from its centre arrives with a redshift as large as one likes. José Lemos and Erick Weinberg named that limit a quasiblack hole.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The dust has mass density $\rho$ and charge density $\pm\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0G}\,\rho$, of one sign throughout, and the metric is $-U^{-2}c^2dt^2 + U^2$ times flat space.
history: A ball of hydrogen in which one atom in about $10^{18}$ has lost its electron neither falls in on itself nor flies apart [bonnor1965]. The protons left over repel one another as strongly as the whole ball pulls on itself by gravity, so it needs no pressure to hold it up [bonnor1965]. The ball is William Bonnor's, written down at Queen Elizabeth College, London, in November 1964 as a reply to Fred Hoyle and Jayant Narlikar [bonnor1965, hoyle1964]. They had maintained that a large mass of gas must go on collapsing until a singularity forms, and much of their case rested on what Bonnor called "the apparent non-existence of plausible equilibrium configurations for large masses" [bonnor1965, hoyle1964]. His sphere of charged dust is such a configuration, and "the mass and radius are arbitrary" [bonnor1965].¶Every grain of the dust carries a charge of $\sqrt{G}$ times its mass, in Gaussian units, the balance that holds Sudhansu Datta Majumdar and Achilles Papapetrou's black holes at rest [bonnor1975, hartle1972]. Does it hold inside matter, where the energy of the electric field has weight of its own [lemos2004]? It does, in the same metric, $-U^{-2}c^2dt^2 + U^2$ times flat space, with the density $\rho$ of the dust as a source for $U$: $$\nabla^2U = -\frac{4\pi G}{c^2}\,\rho\,U^3$$ [bonnor1975, lemos2004]. The shape of the body is free, a freedom already in Papapetrou's solution of 1947 [bonnor1965, papapetrou1947]. The charge is fixed: at the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies in 1962, Anadi Das found static solutions of this kind possible "only if mass density and charge density are equal in magnitude" [das1962]. The equation is easy to solve backwards: guess a $U$, differentiate it, and read off the density, which has only to come out positive [lemos2004].¶Bonnor's guess of 1965 was $U^{-2} = (r_0^3 + mr^2)/(r_0 + m)^3$ inside a sphere of radius $r_0$, with $m = GM/c^2$ for a star of mass $M$ [bonnor1965]. Its density falls from the centre to the surface, and outside the surface the field is Reissner and Nordström's with the charge equal to the mass [bonnor1965]. He called the equilibrium "delicate": "A slightly greater charge density would cause the cloud to expand, and a slightly lesser one would make it contract" [bonnor1965]. The lesson he drew for Hoyle and Narlikar's collapse was that charge "may possibly be able to halt" it [bonnor1965].¶Ten years on the puzzle was the quasars: could a redshift as large as theirs be gravitational [bonnor1975]? For a star of uniform density whose pressure is at most a third of its density the redshift is at most one, at the centre [bonnor1975]. Bonnor and S. B. P. Wickramasuriya tried what they called "electrically counterpoised dust", in a sphere with $U = 1 + (m/2r_0)(3 - r^2/r_0^2)$ inside the coordinate radius $r_0$ [bonnor1975]. Light from its centre arrives redshifted by $3m/2r_0$, and since $r_0$ may be as small as one pleases, "this redshift can be made as great as we please" [bonnor1975]. The star keeps its size as $r_0$ goes to zero: its radius tends to $4m/3$ and its area to $4\pi m^2$, the area of the horizon of the field outside [bonnor1975]. Its central density tends to $2c^2/(9\pi Gm^2)$, so the redshift owes nothing to great density [bonnor1975].¶Their second body was an oblate spheroid of the same dust [bonnor1975]. Flattened to a disc of coordinate radius $a$, it keeps a finite redshift, $\pi m/2a$ [bonnor1975]. Shrunk at a fixed shape, $a \to 0$, its redshift grows without limit while the body keeps a finite size and density, and the field outside it becomes round, $U = 1 + m/r$ [bonnor1975]. Bonnor and Wickramasuriya took that as a plain case of "how a horizon filters out the non-spherically symmetric gravitational and electric fields" [bonnor1975]. The dust of the sphere grows denser toward its surface, and that of the spheroid does over part of it, so they called the stability of both "questionable" [bonnor1975].¶How would anyone outside tell such a star from a black hole [lemos2004]? José Lemos and Erick Weinberg's test of 2004 is a probe sent in and waited for: it comes back, since nothing inside is singular, after a delay that grows without limit as the star nears its horizon [lemos2004]. They named such solutions quasiblack holes, a kind first built from magnetic monopoles, and they named Bonnor and Wickramasuriya's sphere the Bonnor star [lemos2004]. Their own example is a cloud with no edge, $U = 1 + m/\sqrt{r^2 + b^2}$, the extremal black hole itself at $b = 0$ [lemos2004]. The limit is no smooth manifold, and the tidal forces on a body falling through the quasihorizon grow without bound on the way to it [lemos2004]. The same holds in more than four dimensions: Lemos and Vilson Zanchin's Bonnor stars of 2008, squeezed far enough, are quasiblack holes again [lemoszanchin2008].

related.text: The same metric with no dust. Where $\rho = 0$ the potential $U$ is harmonic and its poles are extremal black holes, and the field outside a star of this dust is the single hole's [hartle1972, bonnor1975].
The outside of each spherical star, with the charge equal to the mass, $r_q = r_s/2$. The surface of the star lies outside the horizon, as near it as one likes [bonnor1965, bonnor1975].
The same balance on a thin shell. A shell of dust whose charge equals its mass rests at any radius outside its gravitational radius, with flat space inside it [gao2008].
The star of uniform density, held up by pressure. With its pressure at most a third of its density its redshift is at most one, at the centre, where a star of this dust has no bound [bonnor1975].
Another star with no pressure, held up by the orbits of its particles. Einstein concluded that its Schwarzschild radius lies well inside it [einstein1939, bonnor1975].

Discs of dust in counter rotation, the bodies Bonnor and Wickramasuriya set out from. Their redshift is of order one, and the charged spheroid flattened to a disc keeps a finite redshift too [morgan1969, bonnor1975].

Dimensionless potential inside the sphere, with $\partial_rU = -mrU^3/(r_0 + m)^3$; it is $(1 + m/r_0)^{3/2}$ at the centre and $1 + m/r_0$ at the surface, and the density, $\rho = 3mc^2/\left(4\pi G\left(r_0 + m\right)^3\left(1 + mr^2/r_0^3\right)\right)$, falls from the centre to the surface

coordinates.convention: We use isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ inside Bonnor's sphere of 1965, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. His $f$ is $1/U$ and his radius $a$ is $r_0$ here. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{m\,r}{U^2\left(r_0 + m\right)^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{m\,r\,U^2}{\left(r_0 + m\right)^3}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(m\,r^2\,U^2 - \left(r_0 + m\right)^3\right)}{\left(r_0 + m\right)^3}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(m\,r^2\,U^2 - \left(r_0 + m\right)^3\right)\sin^2\theta}{\left(r_0 + m\right)^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

parameters.description: Mass parameter of the star, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ its mass, a length; its charge is $Q = \pm\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0G}\,M$
Focal radius of the oblate spheroidal coordinates, a length: the surfaces of constant $u$ are spheroids whose foci lie on the ring of radius $a$ in the plane $z = 0$
Surface of the spheroid, $u = u_0 > 0$; its meridional section has eccentricity $1/\cosh u_0$ in the flat background
Dimensionless potential inside the spheroid, with $\partial_uU = -mu^3/(au_0^3\cosh u_0)$; on the disc $u = 0$ it is $1 + (m/a)\left(\arctan(1/\sinh u_0) + u_0/(4\cosh u_0)\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use oblate spheroidal coordinates $(t, u, \theta, \phi)$ inside Bonnor and Wickramasuriya's spheroid, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $x = a\cosh u\cos\theta\cos\phi$, $y = a\cosh u\cos\theta\sin\phi$, and $z = a\sinh u\sin\theta$, so $\theta$ is a latitude and $u = 0$ is the disc of radius $a$ in the plane $z = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use Lemos and Weinberg's harmonic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. Their $R$ is $r$ here, their $q$ is $m$, and their $c$ is $b$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
